newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH PREMIER PRAISES OPPOSITION SPLIT ON BUDGET.
newsitem.headline: CZECH PREMIER PRAISES OPPOSITION SPLIT ON BUDGET.

text.p: Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, facing a cliffhanger vote on the state budget, praised a leading Social Democrat on Wednesday amid signs that an opposition split could hand the government victory.

Klaus said that Social Democrat Jozef Wagner, who chairs the parliamentary budget committee, was putting the interests of the nation first by recommending that deputies approve the 1997 draft budget at its first reading.

Klaus's centre-right coalition, which lost its parliamentary majority in elections last year, has hinted it might resign if the opposition succeeded in forcing changes to the balanced budget in the vote, expected later on Wednesday.
Social Democrat leader Milos Zeman, an enemy of Klaus, has called on deputies to demand amendments to the draft.

In a speech to parliament on Tuesday night, Wagner lambasted the government but ended with a recommendation to pass the budget. "This country needs calm and stability and that will be provided by an approved budget," he said.
Klaus welcomed on Wednesday the signs of the split.
"I have expressed my disagreement with what Mr Wagner said but I also want to appreciate Mr Wagner for suggesting to the chamber that the budget should go to a second reading.
"Mr Wagner showed he understands that the stability of this country is more important than minor political quarrels," Klaus told parliament.
With Senate elections due next month, the political climate is heating up and Klaus has accused the Social Democrats of trying to reverse post-communist reforms.
The three-party coalition holds 99 out of 200 seats in parliament and therefore only needs a couple of opposition defections to win the budget vote.
The Social Democrats' parliamentary leader Stanislav Gross admitted on Tuesday that a couple of his deputies were not happy with changes to the budget which the opposition wanted.

They want amendments to two paragraphs. The first allows the government to change the budget after parliamentary approval provided that overall expenditure and revenue remains unchanged. The second gives limited powers to the mayors of four major Czech cities to change their municipal budgets.

Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik said the first paragraph was purely for the sake of efficient administration. "If there were not this power ... any small organisational change would have to be organised by the chamber. This is not the power to manipulate revenue but a practical matter," he told parliament.
Klaus has not explicitly made the vote a confidence issue. If the government lost, it would have only to resubmit the budget with the changes demanded by the opposition.
But on Monday the coalition issued a statement rejecting any opposition attempt to undermine its authority to govern.
To win, the Social Democrats must vote as a bloc along with the two other oppposition parties, the little-reformed Communists and the far-right Republicans.
Communist leader Miroslav Grebenicek confirmed his party would vote against Klaus. "This government does not deserve the confidence of this parliament," he told the budget debate.
